items.secret_text: {name} stares at their hands. 'There was a patient, Day 1. Twenty-three years old. Shrapnel in the abdomen. I could have saved them. I chose to save someone else instead — someone with better odds. The twenty-three-year-old died alone in the hallway.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: The other survivor takes {name}'s hands. 'You made the call a doctor has to make. The person you saved — they're probably alive because of you.' {name} exhales for what feels like the first time in months.
items.grudge_outcome: 'You played God,' the other survivor says coldly. '{name} looks away. Some confessions aren't met with grace.'
items.expose_outcome: The clinic staff learns of the triage choice. Trust wavers, but the harsh reality of triage is acknowledged.
items.blackmail_outcome: You leverage the doctor's guilt to secure priority medical treatments.
items.keep_outcome: You keep the doctor's confession between the two of you.

items.secret_text: {name} recites it like a log entry — the cadence of someone who has read this statement back to themselves many times. 'We were given a sector assignment, not a description of what was in it. My sergeant said hostiles confirmed, command confirmed, I confirmed. We stacked on the door. By the time I understood what we had walked into, it was already done.' A pause. 'Eighteen people. A family shelter. Three of them were school-age.' Then: nothing else. {name} does not add the part about how they survived. Or the part about the commendation.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The other survivor is quiet for a long time. When they speak it is carefully, the way you speak when you know the words matter. 'I was in a shelter like that once. During the evacuation orders. Someone stacked on our door too, but they hesitated, and that was enough.' They don't reach out. They don't touch {name}'s arm. 'You carried out an order. You didn't write it. The ones who wrote it got medals and died in their beds.' {name} exhales, very slowly, like something has been let out of pressure.
items.grudge_outcome: 'How many?' the other survivor asks. {name} says: eighteen. 'I need you to understand that I know that number,' the survivor says. 'Every time I look at you, I am going to know that number.' They do not leave. But the silence between them from that day on has a specific weight to it — the weight of eighteen — and both of them feel it.
items.expose_outcome: You write it on the watch-board in plain language: eighteen civilians, one family shelter, command orders, one commendation. No commentary. {name} stands in the corridor and reads it without moving for four minutes. Several people read it and say nothing. One person takes the pen and writes below it: we needed to know this. Another crosses that out.
items.blackmail_outcome: You tell {name} you want the tactical weapons stored under their bunk — the ones that weren't declared in the intake inventory. You don't say the words. You look at the board, then at {name}, and {name} understands. The weapons appear in your stores two days later, cleaned and oiled.
items.keep_outcome: You quietly close the storage room door and tell {name}: that stays between us. {name} nods once. Since that day, they take every night watch shift that comes up and they never complain about it. That is their language for thank you, and for something else that has no word.

items.secret_text: {name} admits quietly: 'I've been taking morphine from the supply. Not much — just enough to sleep. I know we might need it for someone who's really hurt. I just... I couldn't take the dreams anymore.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'We've all found ways to cope,' the other survivor says. 'But let's find you a better one. Together.' They sit with {name} until dawn, backs against the cold wall, passing a tin cup of bitter chicory between them while {name} shakes through the longest night of their life.
items.grudge_outcome: 'That morphine could have saved someone in withdrawal,' the other survivor says. 'Someone who was actually trying to get clean.' {name} nods. They have no defense. From that day, every time they walk past the medicine cabinet, they feel the other survivor's eyes on the back of their neck — measuring, always measuring.
items.expose_outcome: You lay the empty vials on the mess table during evening count. Nobody speaks. {name} stands in the silence, hands at their sides, while twenty pairs of eyes do the math on how many doses were lost to one person's nightmares. The infirmary installs a padlocked cabinet the next morning. {name} is the one who welds it shut.
items.blackmail_outcome: You lean close enough to smell the sweat on their collar and whisper: one ampoule a week, uncut, delivered to the second ventilation grate. {name}'s hands tremble as they nod. From now on, they dispense your private supply with the same careful precision they once reserved for the dying. The irony is not lost on either of you.
items.keep_outcome: You take the remaining vials from their hiding place and count them together. Then you build a schedule — half-doses, tapering over three weeks. You sit with {name} through the first night of shaking, and neither of you mentions it again. By the fourth week, they sleep without chemical help for the first time since the exchange.

items.secret_text: {name}'s voice breaks: 'I had two children. The evacuation only had room for one — I had to choose. I chose the younger one. My oldest... I told them I'd come back. I didn't come back.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'No parent should ever have to make that choice,' the other survivor says, holding {name}. 'Your child knew you loved them. That's the only thing that matters.'
items.grudge_outcome: The other survivor is silent for a long time. 'I was the child left behind,' they finally say. 'My parents chose my brother. I survived anyway.' The shared wound doesn't heal — it just becomes visible.
items.expose_outcome: The story works its way through the bunks like a slow infection. Mothers look at {name} differently now, pulling their own children a little closer when they pass in the corridor. Nobody says a word of judgment out loud, but the silence in the mess hall when {name} sits down is heavy and total.
items.blackmail_outcome: You remind {name} that the child they saved still needs a roof and clean water, and that those things aren't free. 'I need two extra shifts on the water pump,' you say. {name} looks at their living child, swallows hard, and nods. They work until their hands bleed, driven by a ghost they can't bury.
items.keep_outcome: You sit in the dark with {name} for an hour, saying nothing. You don't try to absolve them—there is no absolution for this. You just bear witness to the weight of it. When the morning bell rings, {name} stands up, touches your shoulder once, and goes back to being a mother to the living.

items.secret_text: {name} confesses: 'The generator that failed on Day 17 — that wasn't an accident. I rigged it to fail so I'd be the only one who could fix it. I was afraid they'd throw me out if I wasn't useful.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'Fear makes us do stupid things,' the other survivor says. 'But you've fixed more than you've broken since then. We all know that.'
items.grudge_outcome: 'People could have frozen that night because of you,' the other survivor says. 'How do I trust anything you fix now?' The question hangs in the air, unanswered.
items.expose_outcome: You write the truth on the maintenance board for everyone to see. The next time the lights flicker, people don't look at the bulbs; they look at {name}. The mechanic is stripped of their primary tools and demoted to manual labor. They spend their days hauling ash, knowing they broke the one thing that mattered: trust.
items.blackmail_outcome: You corner {name} by the fuel tanks. 'My bunk needs a reinforced lock and a personal heater,' you say. 'You know how to route the power.' The mechanic clenches their jaw, trapped by their own lie. For the rest of the winter, your quarters are the warmest in the shelter, bought with extorted labor.
items.keep_outcome: You look at the patched wiring, then at {name}. 'The next time you're afraid,' you say, 'tell me. Don't break the shelter to prove you can fix it.' {name} exhales a breath they've been holding for weeks. The generator never stutters again, and {name} sleeps beside it every night to make sure.

items.secret_text: {name} admits: 'In the first winter, when we ran out of fuel — I burned books. I burned my own books to keep the children warm. I told them they were damaged anyway. They weren't damaged. They were perfectly good books.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'You kept children alive with paper and ink,' the other survivor says. 'Any author would call that the highest use of their work.' {name} smiles weakly. They'd never thought of it that way.
items.grudge_outcome: 'Books are irreplaceable,' the other survivor says. 'So are children. I don't know which side of this I'm on.' The ambiguity is almost worse than condemnation.
items.expose_outcome: The ashes of the lost library are cataloged in the shelter's archive. The scholars and historians of the settlement refuse to look {name} in the eye. They see a vandal; {name} knows they just see a pragmatist. But when the children ask for stories, the empty shelves are a condemnation that no amount of warmth can excuse.
items.blackmail_outcome: You don't ask for much. Just private tutoring sessions, after hours, focusing on pre-war history. 'You owe the future something, after what you burned,' you tell {name}. The teacher spends their evenings exhausted, reciting memorized texts to you until their voice gives out, paying off a debt measured in pages.
items.keep_outcome: 'Paper is just paper,' you say softly. 'The knowledge is still in your head. Teach them that.' {name} begins holding oral history circles by the glow of the emergency lights. The books are gone, but the stories survive, passed breath to breath in the dark.

items.secret_text: {name} does not whisper. They say it at a normal volume, like ripping something off — the kind of honesty that is exhausted rather than brave. 'The name I gave at intake is not mine. The papers belong to a person who died in the camp processing queue before the second wave. They were still warm. I was shaking too hard to write my own name, and their papers were in my hand, and I wrote what was already there.' A pause. 'I don't know their first name. Just the surname. I have been answering to it for eight months.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: The other survivor looks at {name} for a long time. Then they say: 'What was your actual name?' {name} tells them. It is the first time the name has been spoken aloud in eight months. The listener nods once and says: 'That's who I'll call you. Nobody else needs to know until you're ready.' They don't hug. They don't promise anything. But they remember the real name every single time after that.
items.grudge_outcome: 'That dead person has family somewhere who is still looking for them,' the other survivor says. 'Their family gets a rumor that they survived. They spend years checking reports.' {name} has no defense. They knew this. The silence that follows is the silence of someone who made a choice under impossible pressure and now has to live in its specific shape.
items.expose_outcome: You submit the identity discrepancy to the registry ledger with a note: documents belonged to a deceased individual, current holder is alive and contributing, real name known to administration. You do not post this publicly. You do not make {name} stand in front of anyone. But the registry is accurate now, and that matters for what comes after.
items.blackmail_outcome: You tell {name} what you know. You say you will not act on it — provided their ration allocation is quietly supplemented from the undeclared stores they mentioned last month. {name}'s face does not change much. They were probably expecting this. They nod.
items.keep_outcome: You tell {name}: the name you go by in this bunker is yours. Nobody will hear otherwise from me. {name} is quiet for a moment. Then they say the real name, once, aloud, just so it doesn't disappear entirely. You both agree it was said. Then you agree not to bring it up again.

items.secret_text: {name} stares at the floor: 'The blackout on Day 23 — that was me. I was running an unauthorized line to my bunk, trying to keep a small heater going. The whole grid tripped. I never told anyone it was my fault.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'You've kept the lights on every day since,' the other survivor says. 'One mistake doesn't erase a hundred fixes.'
items.grudge_outcome: 'People panicked in the dark that night,' the other survivor says. 'Someone got hurt. That's on you.' {name} nods slowly. They knew this was coming.
items.expose_outcome: You post the cause of the blackout on the community board. The survivor who broke their arm in the panic during the darkness confronts {name} in the corridor. There is no violence, just a quiet, devastating accounting of pain. {name} moves their bunk to the coldest corner of the shelter that night.
items.blackmail_outcome: You point out the unauthorized tap line. 'Route it to my sector,' you say. 'Nobody else has to know.' {name} spends two days crawling through the ductwork, rewiring the grid to siphon power to your quarters. You sleep in warmth while the rest of the shelter shivers, and {name} carries the guilt of both.
items.keep_outcome: You disconnect the unauthorized line together. 'We share the cold,' you say, 'or we don't survive.' {name} nods, wrapping the copper wire carefully. They become the most meticulous steward of the power grid, balancing the load so perfectly that the main transformer never trips again.

items.secret_text: {name} admits in a whisper: 'During the third week when rations dropped to 400 calories, I skimmed lard and dried fruit into a metal tin behind the boiler. I was keeping it for my daughter in case the soup ran dry completely.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'Any parent would have done the same,' the other survivor says quietly. 'Put it in the communal pot now and we call it square.'
items.grudge_outcome: 'People were fainting at their work stations while you had sugar hidden,' the other survivor says with bitter contempt.
items.expose_outcome: You carry the tins into the mess hall and stack them on the center table during the mid-day meal. No explanation is needed. The colony divides the hoard into pathetic, equal slivers. {name} is relegated to washing pots, forbidden from handling raw ingredients ever again.
items.blackmail_outcome: You visit the kitchen after lights out. 'I like my soup thick,' you whisper, tapping the hidden tin. {name} closes their eyes and nods. From then on, your bowl always has a piece of dried fruit or a scrap of real meat at the bottom, stolen from the mouths of {name}'s family to buy your silence.
items.keep_outcome: You leave the tin where it is, but you log it in a private ledger. 'When the winter gets to its worst,' you tell {name}, 'we use this for the children. Not just yours. All of them.' {name} agrees. When February brings the hardest freeze, that secret tin saves three lives.

items.secret_text: {name} grips their temples: 'The southern highway bridge that collapsed during evacuation — I signed the safety permit under pressure from the ministry. I knew the concrete was substandard. Two hundred civilian vehicles went into the river.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'The bureaucrats threatened to shoot you if you didn't sign,' the listener says. 'The blame belongs to the people who started the war.'
items.grudge_outcome: 'You traded two hundred lives for your pension,' the listener says, turning away in disgust.
items.expose_outcome: The engineering certificate is pinned to the town square bulletin.
items.blackmail_outcome: You demand full structural fortification of your private quarters.
items.keep_outcome: You bury the document and let the engineer rebuild with clean concrete.

items.secret_text: {name} looks at the dirt: 'When the requisitions convoy came through our valley before the exchange, I set fire to our seed barn rather than let the military seize it. I thought the war would end in a week. I burned enough heirloom seed to feed this whole province.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'You were resisting military looting,' the listener says. 'Nobody knew the world was ending tomorrow.'
items.grudge_outcome: 'We could have planted three valleys with what you burned out of spite,' the listener says coldly.
items.expose_outcome: The agricultural loss is entered into the provincial ledger.
items.blackmail_outcome: You demand the remaining secret heirloom seed packet.
items.keep_outcome: You promise to help germinate the few seeds that survived the blaze.

items.secret_text: {name} holds their wooden cross: 'I stopped believing in God the afternoon the second missile blossomed over the harbor. Every eulogy, every blessing I've given in this shelter since Day Zero has been an empty performance. I do it because people need to believe in something.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'Giving comfort when you have none left yourself is the purest definition of grace,' the listener says gently.
items.grudge_outcome: 'You gave us hollow theater while our children were dying,' the listener says with deep bitterness.
items.expose_outcome: The truth of the priest's empty faith spreads like a rot through the shelter. For many, those hollow prayers were the only thing keeping the dark at bay. The makeshift chapel is abandoned by the end of the week. {name} sits alone in the quiet, finally free of the lie, but entirely bereft of a flock.
items.blackmail_outcome: You sit in the confessional. 'You still have their ears,' you say. 'When the council votes on rationing tomorrow, tell them God demands sacrifice from the lower levels.' The priest bows their head, broken. The sermon the next morning is a masterpiece of manipulation, and you get exactly what you wanted.
items.keep_outcome: You sit in the empty pew next to {name}. 'We don't need you to believe,' you say gently. 'We just need you to be here.' {name} looks at the rough wooden cross, then back at you. They continue the rituals, not for a God they can't hear, but for the people they can see.

items.secret_text: {name} unfolds a yellowed manuscript: 'Three weeks before the exchange, I had proof that the municipal bunker ventilation filters were defective. The publisher killed the article after a visit from defense ministry officials. I took the buyout and bought a ticket to the mountains.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'They would have disappeared you into a military prison if you ran it,' the listener says.
items.grudge_outcome: 'Thousands of people choked in those bunkers because nobody warned them,' the listener says.
items.expose_outcome: The pre-war press suppression article is published on the shelter wall.
items.blackmail_outcome: You demand the journalist's pre-war dossier on local faction leaders.
items.keep_outcome: You preserve the original draft for the final historical record.

items.secret_text: {name} stares at the ceiling: 'On Day 2, they ordered our transport wing to fly through the fallout plume to evacuate high command staff. I disabled my aircraft's fuel pump and claimed engine failure. Another crew flew the mission. Their plane melted in midair.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'You refused a suicide run for corrupt politicians,' the listener says. 'That wasn't cowardice, it was sanity.'
items.grudge_outcome: 'Your squadron mates died doing the job you ducked,' the listener says coldly.
items.expose_outcome: The court-martial charge sheet is made known to veteran groups.
items.blackmail_outcome: You extract navigation charts and flight instruments.
items.keep_outcome: You recognize the pilot's right to live and seal the report.

items.secret_text: {name} checks their glasses: 'The radiation water assay on the reservoir during Month Two was five times the permissible limit. I lowered the reported numbers in the official dispatch so people wouldn't riot before the filtration unit was installed.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'Panic in a sealed shelter kills faster than cesium,' the listener says quietly.
items.grudge_outcome: 'People were drinking poison because you treated us like laboratory rats,' the listener screams.
items.expose_outcome: The original water contamination telemetry is exposed.
items.blackmail_outcome: You demand private filtration cartridges for personal use.
items.keep_outcome: You mandate independent water testing while protecting the scientist.

items.secret_text: {name} polishes their rifle barrel: 'During the first winter, a teenage scavenger tried to take two rabbits from my wire snare. He dropped his knife and raised his hands. I shot him anyway. I was so hungry I couldn't see straight.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'Starvation turns human beings into wolves,' the listener whispers in horror. 'God forgive us all for what we became that winter.'
items.grudge_outcome: 'You executed an unarmed kid for two dead rabbits,' the listener says, drawing back in pure revulsion.
items.expose_outcome: The wilderness homicide is reported to the border settlement.
items.blackmail_outcome: You demand prime game cuts and hunting munitions.
items.keep_outcome: You tell the hunter that their debt can only be paid by defending the living.

items.secret_text: A ledger recovered from the merchant syndicate proves the Independent Settlements lost six hundred settlers to famine in Year Two while leadership reported zero deaths to maintain trade leverage.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The syndicate acknowledges the ledger without apologizing for the math. They agree to open the emergency grain reserves, but only at night, and only if the empty sacks are returned.
items.grudge_outcome: The trading posts do not riot. They simply stop extending credit to anyone wearing syndicate colors, and the silence in the markets is louder than a riot.
items.expose_outcome: You nail the ledger pages to the public board at the water exchange. The syndicate's credit rating collapses before noon, and their caravans are turned away at three borders.
items.blackmail_outcome: You agree that the ledger was lost in a fire. The syndicate agrees that your bunker's supply requisition will always be the first one loaded onto the outbound wagons.
items.keep_outcome: You lock the ledger in the deep archive. The syndicate knows you have it, and they know you know they know, which makes every future negotiation very brief.

items.secret_text: An internal Directorate audit reveals military high command inflated regiment headcounts by 40% to claim double food quotas from civilian relief trucks.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The Directorate accepts the correction without admitting fault. They quietly reassign the logistics officers to the front lines and redirect the excess grain to civilian shelters.
items.grudge_outcome: The conscripts on the ration lines do not mutiny, but they stop saluting, and their rifles are suddenly too dirty to fire during drills.
items.expose_outcome: You staple copies of the audit to the checkpoint barricades. By evening, three supply convoys have been blocked by civilians who know exactly how many calories were stolen.
items.blackmail_outcome: You hand over the audit. In exchange, two crates of military-issue cartridges and a box of ceramic armor plates fall off a transport truck near your hatch.
items.keep_outcome: You fold the audit into a sealed envelope. You do not ask for weapons; you ask for a dedicated patrol schedule, and the patrols arrive on time.

items.secret_text: A dead courier's dispatch confirms the Rebel Coalition deliberately introduced brine and heavy metals into the North Oasis well to force local farmers into their partisan ranks.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The rebel council blames a rogue cell and quietly executes three of their own officers. They send a medical detail to the Oasis to treat the heavy metal poisoning.
items.grudge_outcome: The farmers stop selling excess grain to the rebel camps. The camps go hungry, and the farmers sleep with their rifles loaded.
items.expose_outcome: You read the dispatch aloud over the neutral frequency. The farmers burn the rebel banners they had hung in their barns.
items.blackmail_outcome: You demand the codes for the safe-house network and a crate of smuggled rifles. They pay it, but the courier who delivers it does not look you in the eye.
items.keep_outcome: You leverage the silence. Before the week is out, a rebel engineering team arrives at the Oasis and begins installing a commercial reverse-osmosis rig.

items.secret_text: A flight blackbox reveals the Iron Clique welded the blast doors of Bunker 9 shut from the inside while eight hundred civilian women and children hammered on the exterior steel.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The Clique officers admit nothing publicly, but a surveyor calculates the air volume in Bunker 9. They were right: the scrubbers would have failed in forty-eight hours.
items.grudge_outcome: Whenever a Clique patrol walks through a trading post, the locals stop talking. Nobody mentions Bunker 9. The silence mentions it.
items.expose_outcome: You play the blackbox audio over the emergency band. The sound of fists on steel echoes through every radio in the valley, and the Clique's recruitment dries up overnight.
items.blackmail_outcome: You hand over the tape drive. Two days later, a heavy cargo truck drops four barrels of diesel and a set of carbide machine tools at your perimeter.
items.keep_outcome: You keep the tape. The Clique stops sending scouting parties anywhere near your sector, preferring to give a wide berth to the ghost of Bunker 9.

items.secret_text: Signed shipping bills prove the Meridian Compact diverted thirty trucks of civilian burn dressings and antibiotics to their private officers' sanctuary during the first month.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The diplomats do not blink. They explain the logic of state continuity using demographic projections. The math is cold, but the math is correct.
items.grudge_outcome: The border clinics stop accepting Meridian requisition orders. When Compact officers get sick, they have to pay in hard fuel like everyone else.
items.expose_outcome: You pin the shipping bills to the door of the largest Free Clinic. The next day, a Meridian envoy's vehicle is turned over and set on fire in the street.
items.blackmail_outcome: You surrender the original manifests. At the start of every month, a courier delivers a sealed box of iodine, clean bandages, and sterile sutures to your gate.
items.keep_outcome: You keep the bills filed away. The Meridian command knows you have them, which means your people never have to wait in line at the triage tents.

items.secret_text: Encrypted radio telemetry confirms the New Order artillery battery fired the opening salvo that shattered the Year Three Truce, then blamed local raiders.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The Order's liaison explains the first strike as a calculated preemptive necessity. They do not apologize, but they offer you a share of the captured territory's output.
items.grudge_outcome: The surrounding settlements begin digging trenches and laying wire. The Order finds itself surrounded by a circle of loaded rifles.
items.expose_outcome: You hand the telemetry keys to the remaining neutral envoys. The Order is immediately expelled from the regional trade council, and their caravans are shot on sight.
items.blackmail_outcome: You trade the encrypted drives for two crates of heavy mortar shells and a rebuilt diesel generator. The Order considers it a cheap price for their reputation.
items.keep_outcome: You lock the drives in the bunker vault. The Order redraws their expansion maps, meticulously leaving your sector untouched to avoid provoking you.

items.secret_text: An inspection behind the water cistern reveals three cases of canned meat and dried milk carefully set aside by the quartermaster over four months.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The quartermaster breaks down and confesses they were saving it for a winter reserve.
items.grudge_outcome: The shelter demands the quartermaster be removed from supply distribution.
items.expose_outcome: You drag the three cases into the center of the mess hall. The quartermaster tries to explain it was for winter, but hunger has no patience for seasons. They are stripped of their keys, beaten severely by two of the night shift, and banished to the outer airlock duties.
items.blackmail_outcome: You tap the top case with your boot. 'I'm suddenly developing a taste for protein,' you say. From that day forward, the quartermaster's hidden reserve becomes your personal larder. You eat well in the dark, and they sweat every time the inventory books are opened.
items.keep_outcome: You stack the cases back and cover them with the tarp. 'When the ice storms hit, we use these,' you declare quietly. 'Until then, neither of us saw this.' The quartermaster nods, terrified but grateful, locking the secret away in the cold.

items.secret_text: Behind a false cinderblock wall in Sub-Level 2, accessed by pressing the third block from the left at waist height, lies an intact auxiliary room. Four pristine air filters still in their factory packaging. Two medical oxygen tanks, full, valves capped in yellow grease. A sealed crate of potassium iodide tablets, three hundred count. Someone built this wall deliberately, early in the occupation, and put this room behind it. There is a chair inside, facing the tanks. The chair has been used.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The overseer's notes from the first week are found behind the oxygen tanks: 'Biological containment. If it becomes necessary, this room is for the person who cannot be allowed into the main shelter. I will be that person if it comes to that.' The notes are signed with initials. Nobody in the current shelter knows whose they are. The room was prepared by someone who intended to lock themselves inside it. That changes what the room means.
items.grudge_outcome: The two dust storms that came through in Month Three — when six people had pulmonary symptoms for a week and the spare filters ran out — are not forgotten by anyone who lived through them. The oxygen tanks alone would have helped. The filters would have prevented the worst cases. Whoever sealed this room sealed it while people were struggling to breathe in the corridor twenty meters away. The shelter does not forgive that easily.
items.expose_outcome: You tear out the false wall panel by hand, which takes longer than expected because it was well-built. Then you carry the oxygen tanks up the stairwell yourself and set them in the medical bay. Someone counts the iodide tablets and marks the number on the supply board in red. The filters go into the maintenance locker. Nobody says anything about the chair.
items.blackmail_outcome: You seal the panel again. Then you tell the three people most likely to find it that there is nothing behind it — water damage, not worth exploring. The room stays yours. You take the iodide for yourself and leave the tanks where they are. A private retreat, clean air, full oxygen. In this shelter that is a kind of wealth.
items.keep_outcome: You leave the contents in place and update the inventory ledger with a note: emergency auxiliary stores, restricted access, medical emergency only. The room stays locked. You keep one key. You tell one other person — the one you trust most to make the call when the time comes.

items.secret_text: Taped inside an air return duct in the infirmary are six vials of military-grade morphine hidden with a syringe and a tourniquet.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The user confesses and agrees to supervised withdrawal.
items.grudge_outcome: The infirmary locks down all pharmaceutical access.
items.expose_outcome: You pull the tape and let the vials spill out onto the triage cot in full view of the morning clinic line. The trust in the medical staff shatters instantly. The infirmary is subjected to daily invasive searches by the militia, and the hidden user is exiled to the surface before nightfall.
items.blackmail_outcome: You slide four of the vials into your own coat. You leave two behind with a note: 'I'll take the rest next week.' The user in the infirmary becomes your personal indentured servant, terrified of the withdrawal that awaits when you finally empty the stash.
items.keep_outcome: You leave the tape intact but slip a piece of paper into the bundle: 'I know. Come to me when you want to stop.' Three days later, the infirmary assistant knocks on your door, shivering, ready for the painful work of getting clean in secret.

items.secret_text: The security log for Day 42 has a page torn out and rewritten in different ink to hide that the night guard fell asleep while a raider scout surveyed the outer intake grates.
items.forgiveness_outcome: The guard admits exhaustion after seventy hours without sleep and agrees to paired watches.
items.grudge_outcome: The colony demands the guard be assigned to waste disposal duty.
items.expose_outcome: You pin the forged logbook page to the bulletin board alongside a drawing of a raider's knife. Panic spreads through the bunker. The guard is stripped of their rifle and publicly shamed, leaving the colony terrified that the dark is no longer safe.
items.blackmail_outcome: You tap the torn edge of the ledger. 'My bunk duty and my sanitation shifts. For the rest of the year.' The guard nods miserably. You sleep soundly while they work double shifts, terrified you'll reveal the night they left the door open.
items.keep_outcome: You pull the guard aside. 'I saw the ink,' you whisper. 'You need sleep, not a court-martial.' You quietly take their next two night watches, letting them recover without destroying the colony's fragile sense of security.

items.secret_text: {name} keeps the scalpel wrapped in a page of the old triage list, and one night, unwrapping it too slowly, the story comes out with the cloth: 'Nine reached my table that first winter. Four could be saved. I saved four — but I chose them in the order the list was written, top down, and the list was written by rank. The two I skipped were at the bottom because they were nobody. I have operated eleven years since on the excuse that the list was not mine. The hands remember the order anyway. The hands always knew.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'The list was the century,' the other survivor says. 'You were one pair of hands inside it. Four breathed because of those hands, and two of the four were nobody — which means the rank stopped mattering the moment you touched them. That is not absolution. That is the receipt.' {name} folds the scalpel page smaller than usual before putting it away, which is the closest thing to peace the hands have offered in eleven years.
items.grudge_outcome: The room goes cold in the specific way that has nothing to do with weather. Somebody at the back — young, from the north settlements, nobody's child on anybody's list — says very quietly: 'So if it happens again, where do I fall?' {name} has no answer that is also a mercy. The question stays in the sick bay after everyone leaves, sitting on the bench where the patients wait.
items.expose_outcome: The story gets out the way everything gets out here: in pieces, at the water point, deniably. Nobody stops coming to the sick bay — there is no other sick bay — but they come later now, and they watch {name}'s hands instead of their own wounds, and they ask who wrote the list before they ask what hurts. {name} operates exactly as well as before. The room is different. The room was always the patient.
items.blackmail_outcome: You keep the page and the story, and {name} keeps operating — for your people first, at your hours, on your say-so. The best hands in the valley now answer to a piece of folded paper in your pocket. {name} does not hate you for it, which is worse: {name} understands the leverage the way a surgeon understands a clamp, and has quietly begun, you notice, teaching the young ones nothing that would ever need you.
items.keep_outcome: You hear it at 0300 between patients and you say nothing, because nothing was asked for. But after that you start walking the triage line with {name} on bad nights — no lantern, no words, just a second pair of eyes on the order of the list. {name} never mentions it. The lists, from that winter on, are written in {name}'s own hand, and the order in them is the order of wounds. The hands were never the problem. The century was. The century is over.

items.secret_text: {name} is going over the winter ledger a third time when the confession falls out of it like a loose tooth: 'The grain column is padded. Nine percent, every entry, since the first winter — because my arithmetic was wrong in month one and the shelter was four sacks from panic, and I decided the book should carry my error instead of the corridors carrying it. Nine percent. Three winters. I have fed this shelter on a lie measured in sacks, and every full belly in this bunker is downstream of my bad long division.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'So the real number was always nine percent better than we feared,' the other survivor says. 'You didn't steal grain, you stole panic. There's a shelf for that and it's not the one you're reaching for.' {name} laughs once, badly, like a cough — and then, because {name} is {name}, starts a new column that very night: TRUE FIGURES, headed, in the same hand, beside the lie it corrects.
items.grudge_outcome: The grudge finds the only footing it needs: if the grain column lied for three winters, what else did the pencil decide on the shelter's behalf? The question spreads faster than the answer ever could. People start counting their own tins against the board. The board is right — the board was always secretly right — and being right has never once stopped a corridor from keeping its own count.
items.expose_outcome: Exposed, the padding becomes proof of a temperament rather than an error: the shelter learns its quartermaster governs by managed numbers, and every figure on every board now arrives pre-suspected. The grain was always really there. Trust, once the story lands, is nine percent short in every column, including the ones {name} never touched.
items.blackmail_outcome: You hold the error and {name} holds the pencil, which means you hold the pencil. Requisitions you favor move to the top of the stack; the nine percent flows where you point it. {name} signs your slips with the same neat hand that signed the lie, and you both understand the arrangement perfectly: the book was already a fiction. You are simply the newest author.
items.keep_outcome: You sit with the ledger and the liar until the lamp gutters, and what you help {name} build is not forgiveness but a correction: a sealed page, TRUE WINTER FIGURES, countersigned by a second hand — yours — so the truth now has a witness and the witness has a duty. The padding stays secret. The real numbers exist. Somewhere between those two facts is the only honest book in the valley, and only two people know where it is buried.

items.secret_text: The lighter in {name}'s pocket is engraved with a newspaper's masthead, and the story behind it comes out in the dark: 'Before the war I ran a piece — sourced, checked, true in every particular I could verify — about a depot's fuel losses. The paper printed it proud. The authorities read it as a map. The depot's staff were relocated within the month for 'security review,' and relocation, that winter, was a word with a one-way door. My story was accurate. Accuracy was the weapon somebody else picked up. I have not printed a word since, and I carry the masthead anyway, because the pocket should hold something that weighs what it cost.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'You wrote what was true and liars used it,' the other survivor says. 'That's not your crime, that's the century's business model.' {name} turns the lighter over once, thumb on the masthead. 'The families still went through the door,' {name} says — but stays the rest of the night, which is more than {name} has given anyone since. Being forgiven is not the same as being lighter. It is, tonight, two different weights in the same pocket.
items.grudge_outcome: The grudge writes itself in the corridors: the shelter is keeping a professional truth-teller whose one published truth emptied a depot of its people. So every observation {name} makes now arrives pre-audited by fear — what would this become, in the wrong hands, printed? The journalist who survived the war by never writing again survives the peace the same way: accurate, unpublished, and flinching at the sound of a pencil.
items.expose_outcome: The story gets out and does exactly what {name} feared a story would do: it travels faster than its context, arrives in settlements stripped of the eleven years of silence that paid for it, and turns a refugee into an example. Two shelters up-valley start checking their own records against 'the depot journalist.' The truth was accurate. The truth was always accurate. That was never the problem with it.
items.blackmail_outcome: You own the masthead now, which means you own the voice: {name} writes what you want remembered, buries what you want forgotten, and teaches the shelter's record-keeping your grammar. A journalist who fears publication is the perfect instrument of it — every line {name} writes for you is written by someone who knows precisely what words cost. You are not spending that knowledge. You are compounding it.
items.keep_outcome: You hear the whole of it and you ask the only question that matters: 'What should the shelter be writing down?' And {name} — eleven years silent — starts the bunker's record that winter: births, repairs, rations, storms, and one page headed THINGS WE WILL NEED TO REMEMBER ACCURATELY. It is unsigned, unpublishable, and kept in duplicate. The masthead lighter stays in the pocket. The words finally have somewhere to go that isn't a weapon anybody can pick up.

items.secret_text: {name}'s gloves are older than the shelter and softer at the knuckles from worrying them, and the worry has a date on it: 'The evacuation convoy I maintained — forty vehicles, my signature on every inspection card. I found the fault afterward, in my memory the way you find a splinter: a tie-rod on the lead transport I flagged marginal and passed anyway, because the column had to roll before the roads closed. It rolled. The lead transport made the crossing. Three behind it did not keep the schedule it set, in the dark, on a rod I signed. Forty cards. One signature I have been reading for eleven years.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'Marginal passed the load test you gave it,' the other survivor says. 'Three columns behind it met the dark — the dark was already there, waiting on every road. You signed a rod, not a wreck.' {name} does not argue, which is how you know it landed. The gloves stay by the bench. The worrying at the knuckles stops being a habit and starts being, occasionally, just hands thinking.
items.grudge_outcome: The grudge is mechanical, the way {name}'s fears are: if the signature was worth eleven years of worry, what is the rest of the maintenance log worth? Every repaired pump, every shored beam, every card {name} has signed since arrives at the corridors with a hairline question in it. The shelter keeps using the hands — there are no other hands — and keeps, very quietly, a second pair of eyes on the important jobs. {name} notices. {name} notices everything; that is the affliction.
items.expose_outcome: Exposed, the confession becomes a specification: the shelter's mechanic once passed a marginal part, and the part is now every part. Nobody says it to {name}'s face. They say it at the board, about the pumps, in the grammar of procedure — second inspection, dual sign-off, 'given the history.' The rod was signed in a war. The audit is signed every week, forever, in peace.
items.blackmail_outcome: You hold the signature and {name} holds the wrenches, so you hold the wrenches: the shelter's machines get maintained in the order you prefer, and inspections you care about come back clean in the same soft-handed script that once cost eleven years of sleep. {name} does not resent the leverage. That is the telling part — {name} has been waiting, all this while, for someone else to hold the card.
items.keep_outcome: You hear it over a stripped pump at midnight and what you build from it is not comfort but procedure: from that winter, every critical inspection in the bunker carries two signatures — {name}'s and yours — and the second one is not doubt, it is ballast. The lead transport's rod stays signed once, in a war, by one pair of hands that had no second pair. Nothing here will ever be that lonely again. {name} works past midnight more often now, and worries the knuckles less. The gloves are finally just gloves.

items.secret_text: The train ticket book in {name}'s kit is pilot's superstition — a boarding pass for a vehicle that no longer exists — and behind it, one night over the dross of the stove, the flight: 'Nine souls aboard, weight and balance legal, my hand on the throttles the whole way. The manifest said ten. It said ten because a clerk typed ten, and I signed the manifest without walking the cabin, because the weather window was four minutes and the window was God that night. We landed with nine. The tenth name was a typo — a ghost in the paperwork — but for eleven years, on every landing, I have counted the cabin before I open the door. Every time. In case the clerks were right.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'A typo,' the other survivor says. 'You've been haunted for eleven years by a clerk's finger.' {name} almost smiles at it — almost, because the counting is not about the typo, it is about the signature, and the person who hears that hears a pilot who signed for ten and flew with nine and has never once been sure which number was real. 'Nine landed,' {name} says. 'Nine is what I can prove.' It is, the other survivor agrees, a good number. They sit with it like it is a passenger who finally deplaned.
items.grudge_outcome: The grudge latches onto the only tooth it can find: the signature without the walk. A pilot who signs instead of counting. The shelter has no aircraft, which means the story has no use except as a verdict, and verdicts travel: when the winter convoy is planned, somebody at the board says, mildly, that manifests should be walked, and everybody at the table knows which manifest, and {name} knows, and the counting that night at the bunk door takes eleven minutes longer than usual.
items.expose_outcome: The story escapes as stories do — simplified. The valley learns a pilot flew light and lost one and has never said which. The tenth name, the typo, the clerk: none of it survives the water point. What survives is a count that is permanently one short, attached to a person who already counted the cabin eleven years for you. The shelter gains a legend and loses a pilot's sleep, which was thin to begin with.
items.blackmail_outcome: You hold the manifest and {name} holds every convoy plan the shelter will ever need — weights, routes, load discipline, the pilot's eye that sees a bad plan from the air it never flies. The leverage buys all of it, promptly and without argument, because {name} has been carrying an unpaid debt for eleven years and you have simply offered terms. The terms are yours. The debt was always the point; the interest is whatever you decide it is.
items.keep_outcome: You hear the flight, the typo, and the eleven years of counting, and what you give back is a small, ridiculous, load-bearing thing: from that night you walk the bunk line with {name} after lights-out, counting out loud, together — nine, or twelve, or however many the shelter is holding. The count that was one short becomes a count that is always witnessed. {name} still checks the door before opening it. But the counting, for the first time since the weather window, ends when it is supposed to.

items.secret_text: {name} arrived with nothing but the pocket notebook, and the notebook, it turns out, was the nothing that was everything: 'Eleven names. Eleven people paid — food, fuel, a wedding ring, a working dosimeter — for a crossing out of the south that a fixer promised and I organized, because I was the one who could read and write and they trusted the reading and writing. The crossing did not happen. The fixer did not happen. The money happened. I have carried the list eleven settlements instead of walking into any of their families' doors, and I keep it because throwing it away would mean the eleven were only ever a debt I decided to stop paying.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'You were robbed too,' the other survivor says. 'The fixer took the ring and the dosimeter and left you the notebook — left you the eleven names, which is more accounting than the fixer ever kept.' {name} is quiet a long time. 'Accounting isn't payment,' {name} says — but the notebook comes out of the inner pocket that night and moves to the kit bag, which is not forgiveness, and is the first settlement in eleven where the list was allowed to be luggage instead of a wound worn against the skin.
items.grudge_outcome: The grudge does what grudges do with lists: it reads them as rosters. If {name} organized a crossing that never crossed, what else was {name} organizing — and toward the shelter's own door, on what terms? The eleven names become, in the corridors, eleven questions. {name} keeps the bunk and keeps the shifts and loses the thing refugees actually cross valleys for, which is the benefit of the doubt. The notebook goes back to the inner pocket. Against the skin. Where it was.
items.expose_outcome: Exposed, the list becomes a warrant in every settlement that ever lost a crossing: {name} is the one who can read and write, the one who organized, the one who arrived — and arrival, in the valley's grammar, is now indistinguishable from escape. Two families up-road have relatives' names in that notebook. They will hear about it the way everyone hears about everything, wrong-end-first, and they will walk toward this door with the specific patience of people who have waited eleven years for a face to put the weather inside.
items.blackmail_outcome: You hold eleven names and {name} holds nothing else, so you hold {name}: the sharpest road-memory in the shelter, every route and every fixer's face from here to the south, spent at your discretion and logged in nobody's book but yours. {name} walks the routes, counts the caches, names the honest doors. It is good work and it is purchased work, and every settlement {name} passes on your errand is a settlement where the list could still, someday, be read aloud.
items.keep_outcome: You read the eleven names with {name} — all of them, aloud, once, because a list kept in the dark is a debt and a list read is a record — and then you do the only solvent the valley has: you write them into the shelter's own book, under a heading {name} chooses, WHICH WE OWE. The crossing still did not happen. The eleven are no longer a private wound carried between settlements; they are a public obligation with an address. {name} walks the spring trade route asking after families with a notebook full of questions instead of a pocket full of ghosts. Two of the eleven are found that year. The list, at last, is being paid.

items.secret_text: The farm ledger's oldest entries are in {name}'s hand, and the oldest entry is the one {name} cannot leave alone: 'A man on my roster died in the second week — cold, in the north field, on my shift, under my scheduling. I kept him on the roster for eleven weeks. His ration draw kept coming to the board, and his wife and two small ones kept eating it, and the settlement's arithmetic never knew a ghost was feeding them. When the audit came I buried the error in a column nobody reads. I was the overseer. My job was the roster's truth. I falsified the truth for three mouths and I would do it again and that is not the part that keeps me here at the ledger — the part that keeps me is that nobody, in eleven weeks, looked closely enough at the dead man's quota to notice he never missed a shift.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'You kept three alive with a pencil,' the other survivor says. 'The audit kept nobody alive with the truth. I know which one I'd sign for.' {name} closes the ledger on the old column without re-reading it, which is the first time in anyone's memory. 'The roster should have been true,' {name} says — but says it the way a person repeats a rule they have finally, after eleven years, decided was not the highest one on the page.
items.grudge_outcome: The grudge finds the widow first, because grudges do their best work through the people the lie was for: her husband erased from the record, her children fed by an overseer's pencil, her grief administratively postponed for eleven weeks and then quietly annulled. She does not feel rescued. She feels filed. The settlement learns a roster can love you and erase you in the same hand, and every board in the shelter gets read twice from that week on — including, everyone understands, this confession's.
items.expose_outcome: Exposed, the ghost becomes precedent: the overseer who edited the dead is the overseer who can edit the living, and every quota, rotation, and ration line {name} has ever set arrives at the corridors pre-argued. The widow's three mouths were never the scandal — the scandal, it turns out, was the pencil. The shelter keeps the hand it needs and watches it the way you watch weather: useful, load-bearing, and capable of being wrong in columns nobody reads.
items.blackmail_outcome: You own the falsified column, which means you own the column-keeper: rosters that suit you, quotas that lean your way, ghosts of your choosing fed or starved in ledgers nobody audits. {name} signs your arrangements in the same careful hand that signed the dead man's eleven weeks, and the terrible efficiency of it is this — {name} does not even pretend to be corrupted. {name} is, and always was, a person who feeds whoever the pencil points at. You are simply holding the pencil now.
items.keep_outcome: You sit with the ledger and the liar until the true shape of it is on the table between you: not a crime, not a kindness — a ruling. An overseer decided the roster serves the living, and paid for the decision in eleven years of re-reading one column. What you build that night is the shelter's first honest correction: the dead man's name restored to the record with the eleven weeks annotated — DIED IN SERVICE. RATION CONTINUED BY ORDER. FAMILY UNIFORMED. — signed by {name}, countersigned by you. The widow reads it standing. The ghost is discharged. The ledger, for the first time, is both true and merciful, which {name} had been taught, by a colder century, were opposites.

items.secret_text: The recipe tin in {name}'s kit holds no recipe: forty-one letters, folded small, in children's handwriting, confiscated in the last term before the schools closed. 'The authorities took the post,' {name} says. 'Letters home from boarders, letters to fathers at the depots, one to a brother who was already — they told us the mail was suspended for security. A teacher confiscates nothing from a child's heart, so I kept them for return, and the return never came, and I have carried forty-one unsent goodbyes through every settlement since. I teach reading now. Forty-one people's last words to their families are literate because of me and will never be read because of me also.'
items.forgiveness_outcome: 'Suspended mail is not a teacher's sin,' the other survivor says. 'You kept them when keeping them could have cost you. That's not hoarding, that's custody.' {name} opens the tin that night and reads one letter aloud — a boarder's, eleven years old, about a dormitory mouse named Commissar — and laughs, and cries, in the same breath, which the shelter has learned by now is one weather. Forty is a smaller number than forty-one. Nobody explains why. Everybody knows.
items.grudge_outcome: The grudge is quiet and administrative: a tin of other people's words, kept for eleven years, is a tin of other people's secrets — and whose hand, the corridors wonder, chose which letters stayed folded? The children grew up; the families moved or died or are out there, and the post office of the valley is apparently one recipe tin with a jealous custodian. {name} keeps teaching. The tin stops coming out of the kit when others are watching, which is the first step of a long, slow confiscation in reverse.
items.expose_outcome: Exposed, the letters become what the century always turned letters into: evidence. Two are recognized at the water point — a sister's handwriting, a brother's mouse — and the families arrive at your door with eleven years of postponed grief and one question each, and every question is the same: why did the reading of this wait until now? {name} has no answer that is not also the whole confession. The confession, read aloud in the corridors, becomes the shortest version of itself, which is: a teacher kept the mail.
items.blackmail_outcome: Forty-one letters, forty-one threads into families and settlements across the valley — and you hold the tin. {name} reads for you now: which families endure, which bloodlines still answer to which names, which old loyalties a folded page could still wake. It is the finest intelligence the valley contains, gathered by children who trusted a teacher with their hearts, spent by a teacher who has learned, at last, exactly what confiscation means from the other side of the desk.
items.keep_outcome: You and {name} spend the winter doing the only thing the century never permitted: you answer them. Not send them — the post is ash — but read each one aloud, once, to the shelter's own book, and write beside each a line in {name}'s hand: DELIVERED, IN THE CLEAR, TO WHOEVER KEEPS THIS. The boarders' goodbyes reach an audience at last, eleven years late and exactly on time, because the valley's newest generation sits in the corridor school learning to read with real letters, in real children's handwriting, about a real mouse named Commissar. The tin stays open now. Forty-one letters, read. A teacher's confiscation, ended the only way confiscations end — by giving the words back to the world that took them.
